background.definition: Fibrocystic breast disease is a heterogeneous group of benign breast disorders considered to be variations of normal. It is characterized by dense, bumpy, and irregular consistency and associated with cyclic mastalgia.

list.listitem: Fibrocystic disease primarily affects women between the ages of 30 and 50 years; it is rare in postmenopausal women.
The incidence is lower in women taking birth control pills. Family history and diet (excessive intake of caffeine and fat) may influence the incidence, but are controversial risk factors.
Sixty-eight percent of women of reproductive age have some degree of fibrocystic breast disease.
Eleven percent to 22% report moderate-to-severe cyclic mastalgia.
The etiology of fibrocystic disease is unknown. Changes may be associated with hormonal fluctuations of the menstrual cycle and usually subside with menopause.
A heterogeneous group of benign breast disorders including exaggerated cyclic effects, proliferative effects, and involutional effects

Proliferative effects (seen on histology) include epithelial and intraductal epithelial proliferation, lobular hyperplasia, and proliferation of intralobular connective tissue causing an irregular consistency
Involutional effects on lobules produce cysts and sclerosing lesions. Involutional effects on ducts produce dilation, periductal fibrosis, and sometimes nipple discharge.
Among patients with polycystic ovary syndrome, those with a hyperandrogenemia phenotype had a lower risk of fibrocystic disease.
Fibrocystic disease encompasses a heterogeneous group of benign breast disorders often presenting as poorly localized bilateral cyclic breast pain radiating to the axilla. C

In the evaluation of breast pain or fibrocystic breasts, women older than 35 years, women at any age for whom ultrasound results are abnormal or equivocal, and those in whom a dominant mass is identified should have a mammogram. C

Strongly consider core needle breast biopsy or excisional breast biopsy in women with indeterminate breast changes or lumps. Always perform core needle breast biopsy or excisional breast biopsy in women with discrete masses. A

list.listitem: Breast pain is the most common presenting symptom of fibrocystic breast disease. The history should include the location and severity of the pain, relationship to the menstrual cycle, physical activities, and interference with routine activities. Consider pregnancy, use of hormonal contraceptives or hormonal therapy, and use of any medications (eg, spironolactone) in the evaluation of breast pain. Reproductive, medical, and family history should be obtained for further consideration of breast cancer risk.

Breast changes fluctuate with a woman's menstrual cycle, with other hormonal influences experienced during the life cycle (eg, contraception therapy, pregnancy, breastfeeding, hormone replacement therapy, and menopause) and with lifestyle factors.

Three categories of breast pain (mastalgia) should be differentiated based on the history: cyclic (premenopausal women, pain related to time in menstrual cycle, bilateral breasts, and upper outer quadrants; can be unilateral or more intense in one breast); noncyclic (postmenopausal older women, continuous or intermittent pain not associated with menstrual cycle, inner quadrants, localized, and unilateral); and non-mammary (non-breast-related pain, derived from chest wall or alternative site).

The physical examination includes inspection and palpation of breasts, areolar complexes, and regional lymph nodes in supine and sitting positions. The cervical, thoracic spine, chest wall, shoulders, heart, lungs, and abdomen should be examined to rule out nonmammary causes of pain.

Findings on breast examination typically consist of dense tissue with irregular "cobblestone" consistency, more marked in the upper outer quadrants of the breast, which can fluctuate with hormonal changes in the menstrual cycle. Mobile non-anchored breast masses that are rubbery, round, and smooth are also typical. Dense breasts may make breast examination and interpretation difficult. Physical examination can be repeated in 2 to 4 months if these benign findings are initially observed.
Laboratory tests are not useful. A pregnancy test can be obtained to evaluate for pregnancy. Hormone levels of estrogen and progestin are usually normal.
The likelihood of malignancy is very low in women with mastalgia alone. In one series of 987 women referred for breast pain with no mass or other abnormality, only 0.4% had malignancy.

Ultrasound can help distinguish benign from malignant lesions. Breast Imaging-Reporting and Data System (BI-RAD), a risk assessment and quality assurance tool, is used to categorize breast findings in mammography, ultrasound or MRI. For ultrasound, the breast is evaluated for composition, mass, calcifications, associated features and special cases and assigned a category from 0 (needs additional imaging) to 5 (highly suspicious findings present). Scoring breast ultrasound findings for malignancy based on BI-RADS appears to have high accuracy for ruling in cancer.

Mammography should be performed to differentiate benign breast changes from breast cancer and to evaluate nipple abnormalities (eg, nipple discharge or retraction). Perform mammography on women older than 35 years, women at any age for whom ultrasound results are abnormal or equivocal, and those in whom a dominant mass is identified. Nine percent to 22% of palpable breast cancers are not confirmed on mammography; therefore, follow-up and clinical correlation with ultrasound-guided core needle breast biopsy or excisional biopsy are advised.

Breast biopsy should be performed for further evaluation of any dominant masses, especially suspicious fixed nonmobile breast lumps or masses not explained otherwise. A directed ultrasound may be performed to investigate a suspicious mass if physical examination findings are indeterminate. Breast cyst needle aspiration can be performed on large breast cysts. If the aspirate is bloody or there is residual mass, referral for biopsy is required.

Shear wave elastography is under investigation for differentiating between benign and malignant breast masses. Mean elasticity values are lower for fibrocystic changes than for breast lesions such as fibroadenoma, intraductal papilloma, and adenosis or stromal fibrosis; variability, however, is high.
See chapter on breast mass.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to management.
Treat mild disease and benign findings on clinical examination with reassurance; perform mammography/ultrasound, if indicated. B
Suggest a trial of lifestyle changes (eg, hot packs; cold packs; massage; supportive bra; reduction in dietary fat, caffeine, and salt). B
NSAIDS and/or oral contraceptives (OCs) can be used to reduce breast pain. B
Danazol (100–400 mg daily) administered in the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle relieves breast pain in 75% to 92% of women. B

Tamoxifen and possibly evening primrose oil are beneficial in patients with noncyclic mastalgia, although known harms and adverse effects of tamoxifen limit its usefulness. Authors of a systematic review of 9 trials comparing tamoxifen with placebo for chronic mastalgia found a significantly better response with tamoxifen (RR 2.04, 95% CI 1.5 to 2.8).
Analgesics such as NSAIDs are effective in reducing cyclic breast pain.
An OC with a reduced estrogen component can be effective in reducing symptoms.

Danazol, an antigonadotropin agent, can be administered in the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. Danazol (100–400 mg daily; typically, 200 mg daily) relieves cyclic breast pain in 75% to 92% of women. Side effects include acne, hair loss, a decrease in voice pitch, weight gain, depression, and an increase in thromboembolic events. Poor quality of existing RCTs, few comparison trials with other agents, and natural history of spontaneous resolution of symptoms limit applicability of results to all women with mastalgia.

Bromocriptine reduces serum prolactin levels and decreases breast pain by 54% in women with cyclic mastalgia. Dose-related side effects include nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness, and fatigue. Initiating dose is 1.25 mg daily increased to 2.5 mg daily as needed. Bromocriptine benefits persist 3 months to 6 months following treatment discontinuation.

Tamoxifen (10–20 mg daily) has demonstrated effectiveness in the treatment of severe cyclic breast pain (75%–90% reduction in pain) or noncyclical breast pain (56% reduction in pain). Side effects include hot flashes, menstrual irregularity, vaginal dryness, risk of thromboembolism, and risk of endometrial cancer; side effects are dose related.

Authors of a meta-analysis identified 10 studies with 931 patients who had largely cyclical mastalgia and were randomized to 10 to 20 mg tamoxifen daily or either placebo, danazol, or centchroman (a selective estrogen receptor modulator). Compared with placebo (3 studies, 155 patients), patients taking tamoxifen were significantly more likely to experience a 50% or greater reduction in the mean pain score (RR 2.0, 95% CI 1.5 to 2.8). There were non-significant trends favoring tamoxifen over active comparators.

In an RCT trial of 154 women with ultrasound verified fibrocystic breast disease, 90 of whom had baseline pain, a 50% or more reduction in pain was more likely in the group randomized to metformin 500 mg twice daily vs. placebo (63.8% vs 44.2%, p = 0.03, NNT = 5).
Antibiotics, vitamins, and diuretics are not effective for the treatment of mastalgia. Medroxyprogesterone has variable effectiveness on mastalgia in studies.
Experimental drugs effective for breast pain in preliminary clinical trials include goserelin, gestrinone, buserelin, leuprolide, quinagolide, cabergoline, thyroxine, and topical NSAIDs.
The use of herbal preparations and vitamin supplements (eg, vitamin B6, vitamin E) for breast pain is controversial.

Evening primrose oil (2 tablets of 500 mg 3 times a day for 3–4 months) has demonstrated mixed results in RCTs in improving noncyclic and cyclic breast pain. A high content of gamma-linoleic acid is observed to reduce the ratio of saturated/polyunsaturated fat and, in turn, reduces hormone sensitivity.
The effectiveness of dietary interventions (eg, a reduction in saturated fat) is unclear.

A large prospective Chinese study found that a diet rich in fruits and vegetables may reduce cellular proliferation in the mammary epithelium in women with fibrocystic breast disease with or without a history of proliferative breast changes; this is one mechanism by which such a diet could reduce risk of breast cancer.
A professionally-fitted sports bra for activities and a soft supportive bra for sleep are helpful in relieving breast pain.
Lifestyle changes, including smoking cessation, caffeine, and stress reduction, hot packs, cold packs, and improved coping skills, are effective in symptom reduction.
Refer the patient for comprehensive diagnostic evaluation if there are any new, unusual, or dominant lumps.

There is no evidence that fibrocystic disease increases the risk of breast cancer. B In fact, in one study of women with small (≤1.0 cm) node-negative (T1a,bN0) invasive breast cancer, presence of fibrocystic disease was significantly associated with survival.
A pain diary using a visual analog scale can be useful to assess frequency, duration, and intensity of pain to optimize response to therapy. C
The use of hormone therapy in postmenopausal women does not appear to influence the clinical pattern of benign breast disease.
Fibrocystic disease is a normal variant of changes in breast tissue sometimes associated with symptoms that have a negative influence on a woman's quality of life and function.
Evaluate all breast lumps and any persistent breast changes that follow a menstrual cycle.

Hormonal changes and lifestyle factors contribute to the development of fibrocystic breasts. Consider all modifiable risk factors and treatment modalities (eg, caffeine and salt reduction, NSAID trial).
